intro: In this college you'll learn how to go to the doctor in the Netherlands: understand consultation hours, make an appointment, describe how you feel and what hurts, name the parts of your body, and pick up your medicine at the pharmacy.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome — the Dutch doctor system
paragraphs.text: Welcome to theme seven. Its title is [[Naar de dokter]], which means 'to the doctor'. Going to the doctor is something everyone needs sooner or later, and in the Netherlands the system works in a special way, so let's understand it first. Your main doctor is the family doctor, called the [[huisarts]]. You always go to your [[huisarts]] first, for almost everything — you do not just walk into a hospital. If you need a specialist, the [[huisarts]] sends you. To see your doctor, you usually call during the consultation hour, which is called the [[spreekuur]]. So a very useful sentence is [[Wanneer is het spreekuur?]], meaning 'when is the consultation hour?'. The place where you wait is the [[wachtkamer]], the 'waiting room'. In this college I explain everything in English, but every Dutch word and sentence you hear is spoken by a native Dutch voice, so you also train your ear. Please repeat each phrase out loud after me — speaking your symptoms clearly really matters at the doctor. One more cultural note: register with a [[huisarts]] near your home as soon as you arrive, because you need one before you get sick. Are you ready? [[Laten we beginnen!]]

paragraphs.heading: Making an appointment
paragraphs.text: The first thing you do is make an appointment, which in Dutch is [[een afspraak maken]]. When you phone the doctor's office, the assistant answers. You say very simply [[Ik wil graag een afspraak maken]], which means 'I would like to make an appointment'. You can add who it is with, like this: [[Ik wil graag een afspraak maken met de dokter.]] The assistant will usually ask what is wrong, with the question [[Wat is er aan de hand?]], meaning 'what is the matter?'. You give a short reason, for example [[Ik voel me al een paar dagen niet goed]], 'I haven't felt well for a few days'. They may offer you a time today and ask [[Kunt u vandaag langskomen?]], 'can you come by today?'. To say yes, simply answer [[Ja, dat is goed]], 'yes, that is fine'. If the time does not suit you, you can ask [[Heeft u iets in de middag?]], 'do you have something in the afternoon?'. Remember to bring your insurance card, the [[verzekeringspas]] — they often ask [[Heeft u uw verzekeringspas bij u?]]. And if it is a true emergency, you do not call the doctor: you call the national number with [[Bel 112 als het een noodgeval is.]]

paragraphs.heading: Saying how you feel and what hurts
paragraphs.text: Now the heart of this theme: telling the doctor how you feel. The basic sentence is [[Ik voel me niet goed]], which means 'I don't feel well'. If it is more serious you can say [[Ik ben ziek]], 'I am ill', and to say how long, use [[Ik ben al een week ziek]], 'I have been ill for a week'. To talk about specific pain, the key pattern is [[Ik heb pijn aan mijn]] plus a body part — 'I have pain in my'. For example [[Ik heb pijn aan mijn rug]], 'I have pain in my back', or [[Ik heb pijn aan mijn buik]], 'I have pain in my belly'. There is also a neat shortcut: glue the body part onto the word for pain. So a headache is [[hoofdpijn]], a sore throat is [[keelpijn]], and a stomach ache is [[buikpijn]]. You just say [[Ik heb hoofdpijn]], 'I have a headache'. Two more symptom words you will need constantly: fever is [[koorts]], as in [[Ik heb koorts]], and to cough is [[hoesten]], as in [[Ik hoest veel]], 'I cough a lot'. The doctor may ask how long it has been going on with [[Hoe lang heeft u al klachten?]], 'how long have you had complaints?' — that word for complaints, [[klachten]], is the standard medical word here.

paragraphs.heading: The parts of the body
paragraphs.text: To describe pain well, you need the parts of the body, so let's learn them. Let's start at the top: the head is [[het hoofd]], the eye is [[het oog]], the ear is [[het oor]], the nose is [[de neus]], and the mouth is [[de mond]]. The throat, which gets sore so often, is [[de keel]]. Moving down: the neck is [[de nek]], the shoulder is [[de schouder]], and the arm is [[de arm]]. Your hand is [[de hand]] and your fingers are [[de vingers]]. In the middle of your body, the back is [[de rug]], the belly is [[de buik]], and the heart is [[het hart]]. Lower down, the leg is [[het been]], the knee is [[de knie]], and the foot is [[de voet]]. Now combine these with the pattern from before. If your tooth hurts, you say [[Ik heb pijn aan mijn tand]], and a toothache is simply [[kiespijn]]. If you twisted your ankle, you might say [[Ik heb pijn aan mijn voet]]. Another natural way to say something hurts is [[Mijn keel doet pijn]], 'my throat hurts', or [[Mijn rug doet zeer]], which also means 'my back hurts'. Practise pointing at your own body and naming each part out loud — it fixes the words quickly.

paragraphs.heading: Modal verbs: moeten and mogen
paragraphs.text: When the doctor gives advice, you will hear two small but powerful verbs again and again: [[moeten]] and [[mogen]]. [[Moeten]] means 'must' or 'have to', and [[mogen]] means 'may' or 'be allowed to'. The trick with these verbs is that the second verb jumps to the end of the sentence and stays in its basic form. So the doctor says [[U moet veel water drinken]], 'you have to drink a lot of water' — notice 'drinken', the verb for drinking, sits right at the end. Another classic instruction is [[U moet rusten]], 'you have to rest'. About your medicine you will hear [[U moet de medicijnen drie keer per dag innemen]], 'you have to take the medicine three times a day'. Now [[mogen]] is for permission. To ask politely you start with it: [[Mag ik vandaag naar buiten?]], 'may I go outside today?'. And the good news arrives as [[U mag morgen weer werken]], 'you are allowed to work again tomorrow'. You can also use [[moeten]] to ask about yourself: [[Moet ik medicijnen halen bij de apotheek?]], 'do I have to get medicine from the pharmacy?'. Listen for these two verbs — they tell you exactly what you must do and what you are allowed to do.

paragraphs.heading: The pharmacy — and a real phone call
paragraphs.text: After the doctor, you often go to the pharmacy, the [[apotheek]], to collect your medicine. The doctor gives you a prescription, a [[recept]], and you hand it over there. A useful question is [[Heeft u dit medicijn op voorraad?]], 'do you have this medicine in stock?'. Here is a real Dutch habit: for everyday pain and fever, people reach for [[paracetamol]] first — you buy it cheaply at any [[drogist]] or supermarket, and doctors often advise it instead of stronger medicine. Now let's put a whole phone call together. You ring the office and say [[Goedemorgen, ik wil graag een afspraak maken]]. The assistant asks [[Wat is er aan de hand?]] You answer [[Ik heb al drie dagen koorts en pijn in mijn keel]]. She offers [[Kunt u vanmiddag om half drie komen?]], 'can you come at half past two this afternoon?'. You say [[Ja, dat is goed, dank u wel]]. Simple, polite, done. When you leave the doctor, a warm thing to hear is [[Beterschap!]], which means 'get well soon'. So practise your symptoms out loud today, and don't worry about being perfect — doctors are used to helping new speakers. [[Heel goed gedaan, en beterschap!]] Well done — I'll see you in theme eight!
